lessons.title: API contracts and source attribution
lessons.prepare: Official Python open/csv documentation, Python editor, disposable practice folder, week 8 module design and project-workbook.md section 7. Use synthetic data only.

slides.title: API contracts and source attribution
slides.notes: Success means explain an API beyond web services, identify inputs, outputs, side effects and likely errors from documentation, then record a reused source and the learner’s own contribution. This is the scheduled API/attribution lesson, before two project build workshops later in week 9.
body: Unit 1 · Week 9 · Lesson 1
Use a documented interface and explain reused work.

slides.title: Retrieval: module agreements
slides.notes: Allow silent recall, then compare with the week 8 design. order_cost takes a valid quantity and returns integer cents. save_order changes persistent storage and needs an agreed failure signal. An unfinished stub deliberately raises NotImplementedError. Use responses to connect student-defined interfaces to library interfaces.
body: What does order_cost receive and return?
Which module changes the saved file?
How should the caller learn that saving failed?
Compare your module contracts with a partner.

slides.title: An API is a software interface
slides.notes: API means application programming interface. Programs use documented operations supplied by another component. Python’s open and the csv library are local examples. A web API adds remote communication, but this project needs no account, key or network service. The operation contract describes allowed inputs, results, side effects and errors. Ask learners to classify their own function contract and a library call without assuming all APIs use the internet.

slides.title: Documentation detective
slides.strategy: Paired documentation reading and jigsaw explanation
slides.notes: Open the official open and csv.writer documentation linked in the teacher notes. One partner finds file mode, encoding and errors, the other finds writer creation, writerow and newline guidance. Partners explain and complete a four-part contract. Expected: append mode retains existing records, newline="" lets csv control record newlines, encoding="utf-8" makes encoding explicit, writerow receives a row sequence and writes it. Creation of a writer alone does not write a row. open can raise OSError, including PermissionError. Do not copy the entire documentation or memorise every optional parameter. Sources: https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open and https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.writer
body: Find the required input and a useful option.
Identify the returned object and the file side effect.
Find a documented error or failure to handle.
Explain your findings to your partner.

slides.title: A local API in use
slides.notes: Use only a disposable practice folder. This original demonstration appends A01,2,600 as one CSV row. Predict before running, inspect the text file, then change the ID to A02 and quantity/cost to 0 and 0. Both rows should remain. Re-running the unchanged snippet appends a duplicate, so discuss who controls repeated calls. csv writes the record separator, so do not add a separate newline field. The API can quote commas, but the agreed project ID restrictions still apply. The snippet assumes valid values and a writable folder; it is not a complete save_order implementation and has no failure handler. Explain that validation, caller policy and exception handling remain project responsibilities. Sources: official csv and open documentation.
body: Predict the saved row, then inspect the file.
Change the synthetic order and check both rows remain.
slides.code:
import csv
with open("api-practice.csv", "a",
          newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    writer = csv.writer(file)
    writer.writerow(["A01", 2, 600])

slides.title: A useful source log
slides.strategy: Worked example and independent source review
slides.notes: Model a real log entry for this lesson: Source: CS ATAR textbook, Unit 1 Week 9 Lesson 1, site URL and access date. Reused section: original csv practice snippet. Code licence: MIT, retaining the linked copyright/permission notice when distributing reused code. Changes: A01 to A02 and quantity/cost to zero. Own contribution: prediction, run evidence and interface explanation. Then record official Python documentation separately as a consulted reference, with URL, section, access date and what it informed; distinguish consulting documentation from copying its examples. Students audit one actual source from their work and record borrowed section, relevant permission/conditions, changes, own work and permitted assistance in workbook section 7. Follow school rules if used for assessment. If permission is unclear, use an approved source or ask the teacher before reusing. Crediting a source alone does not establish reuse permission.
body: Record the author/title, URL and date accessed.
Identify what you used and its licence or permission.
Describe your changes and your own contribution.
Log one real source in workbook section 7.

slides.title: Credit and permission
slides.strategy: All-student hinge question and scenario discussion
slides.notes: Correct B. Being publicly visible does not itself establish permission to copy and distribute. Naming the author is attribution, while the licence/permission sets conditions. Avoid a blanket judgement about all classroom copyright exceptions: here the question concerns publishing copied code in the shared textbook/project. Students should use an approved licensed alternative or seek guidance, then record required credit. This is a practical source review, not a new legal or assessment policy.
body: You want to publish copied code with your project.
The page names its author but gives no reuse terms.
A: Naming the author alone settles permission.
B: Check permission and conditions before reuse.

slides.title: Exit ticket: an interface you can justify
slides.notes: Collect a short contract for csv.writer/ writerow or open: supplied input, result/effect and a relevant failure. Students explain why csv does not enforce the project’s non-negative quantity rule or determine its save-failure policy. Check a completed source entry distinguishes reused material from original work. Next lesson is error classification and debugging; leave full project storage implementation to the scheduled build workshop.
body: Describe one API call’s input and result or effect.
Name a failure your program must respond to.
Explain one rule the project must still enforce.
Submit your source entry and own contribution.

lessons.title: Error classification and debugging
lessons.prepare: Python editor, project workbook test table and week 8 predicted tests. Use the original small faulty snippets in the slides; no changes to live assessment tasks or important data.

slides.title: Error classification and debugging
slides.notes: Success means distinguish syntax errors, execution exceptions and incorrect logic, reproduce a fault with a small case, find the first incorrect state and verify a correction with retests. This is a guided debugging lesson before the week 9 project build workshops.
body: Unit 1 · Week 9 · Lesson 2
Find the cause of a failure and verify the repair.

slides.title: Retrieval: a contract predicts behaviour
slides.notes: Allow silent answers before comparison. A contract describes inputs, results/effects and errors. A successful run may still calculate the wrong result. Expected results must come from the requirement and independent calculation. A broad handler does not repair an incorrect algorithm. Connect this lesson to last lesson’s API contracts and the existing project tests.
body: What should an operation’s contract tell its caller?
Can a program finish and still give a wrong answer?
Where should an expected result come from?
Compare one example with a partner.

slides.title: Three kinds of failure
slides.notes: Give three original examples verbally or in the editor: if quantity >= 0 with no colon causes SyntaxError; [2,0,5][3] causes IndexError during execution; quantity + 300 instead of quantity * 300 produces a wrong cost without necessarily raising an exception. Learners classify independently, then justify with when and how the fault appears. SyntaxError is a Python exception class too, but distinguish parsing failure from exceptions during ordinary execution for this teaching classification. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/errors.html

slides.title: A traceback narrows the search
slides.notes: Before running, ask for valid list indices: 0, 1 and 2. The call raises IndexError at quantities[3]. In the actual editor show the traceback’s final exception type and the source line, noting wording can vary by Python version. Do not fix the index by guessing or hide the fault with a blanket except. For a required final element, len(quantities)-1 or -1 is valid only after deciding how empty data should behave. Students reproduce with three items, then discuss the empty case. Source: Python errors tutorial.
body: Predict the valid indices, then run.
Read the exception type and the source line.

slides.title: The first incorrect state
slides.notes: The requirement is total quantity 7 for [2,0,5]. This faulty loop prints 5. Trace after each iteration: expected totals 2,2,7 versus actual 2,0,5. The first divergence is after quantity 0. total = quantity replaces the total rather than accumulating. Change only the cause to total += quantity, then rerun. Retest [], [0], [4] and [2,0,5] expecting 0,0,4,7. Learners predict before executing and retain the failed trace as evidence.
body: Expected total: 7. Trace every iteration.
At which iteration does the total first go wrong?
slides.code:
quantities = [2, 0, 5]
total = 0
for quantity in quantities:
    total = quantity
print(total)

slides.title: Paired debugging clinic
slides.notes: Assume the function receives a validated non-negative integer. It should return quantity times 300 cents. This original faulty version adds 300. Predict results for 0,1,4 before running: expected 0,300,1200 and faulty 300,301,304. Navigator identifies the first mismatch and proposes one change; driver edits to quantity * 300, runs all cases and records results. Swap roles, then reuse the previous loop tests including empty data. Record symptom, smallest failing case, cause, correction and retest in the workbook. Support: supply a two-column expected/actual table. Extension: explain how a negative-input contract would need a separate explicit decision; do not silently expand this exercise’s assumptions.
body: Expected cents for quantities 0, 1, 4: 0, 300, 1200.
Predict, reproduce, isolate, repair and retest.

slides.title: A repair needs regression checks
slides.notes: Correct B. The failed case must now pass, and earlier cases should still pass after the change. Re-running previous tests checks for regressions, though a finite set does not prove every possible input. Ask for an empty or zero case that could fail after an apparently sensible change. If students choose A, demonstrate a special-case patch returning 0 for every quantity: it passes quantity zero but fails quantities 1 and 4.
body: You fixed the zero-quantity cost case. What next?
A: Submit because that case now passes.
B: Rerun it and the earlier ordinary/boundary tests.
Choose and justify the evidence a repair needs.

slides.title: Exit ticket: explain a fresh fault
slides.notes: Requirement: accept every whole-number quantity >= 0. The condition > 0 wrongly rejects zero, so this is a logic error. >= 0 is the correction for this isolated range fragment, which assumes successful integer conversion. Tests -1,0,1 should reject, accept, accept. Ask students to distinguish this from int("three") raising ValueError. Collect a precise cause and retest plan, not just a category name. Use gaps to plan support in the calculation/input workshop next lesson.
body: Requirement: accept whole quantities of zero or more.
Classify the fault, correct it and propose three tests.

lessons.title: Calculation and input workshop
lessons.prepare: Open the design chapter and its learning resources. Use paper or a local editor as appropriate, with fictional data and disposable practice copies. The suggested 55-minute lesson is flexible.

slides.title: Calculation and input workshop
body: Unit 1 · Week 9 · Lesson 3
Connect validated input to a tested cost calculation.
slides.notes: Explain the goal and the expected independent outcome. Connect validated input to a tested cost calculation. This is ungraded textbook learning. Suggested times can be adjusted to the class. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Retrieval and explanation
body: What should quantity zero mean?
Where should input conversion happen?
slides.notes: Zero is valid and costs zero cents. Conversion and range checks belong at the input boundary. A calculation function receives a validated quantity. Allow silent thinking before discussion. Ask a learner to justify an answer before revealing the explanation. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: The order contract
table: Whole quantity of zero or more
slides.notes: Use the project requirements. Keep prices in integer cents. No need to add accounts or a new interface. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Predicted costs
body: Predict costs for quantities 0, 1 and 4.
Identify the input and returned result.
slides.notes: Expected costs are 0, 300 and 1200 cents. Ask learners to predict before running. The calculation assumes successful validation. Pause for predictions before discussing the expected result. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Retry trace
body: Trace inputs "three", "-1", "0".
Which input reaches the calculation?
slides.notes: Conversion fails for three. Negative one converts but fails the range rule. Zero is accepted and costs zero. Use driver/navigator roles, then swap. Swap explaining and checking roles so both learners articulate the reasoning. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Independent practice
body: Complete the input and calculation modules.
Test invalid text, a negative value, zero and four.
Record predicted and actual results.
slides.notes: Use a separate project copy. Accept equivalent function names. Check the retry loop actually continues and the calculation returns a value. Support with the chapter example, then ask for an independent changed input. Offer the relevant worked example if needed, then use a changed case to check independent understanding. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: A choice to explain
body: The function prints 1200 but returns no value.
A: The caller receives 1200.
B: The caller receives None.
slides.notes: B. Printing displays text. A normally completed call without an explicit returned value gives None. Ask what cost = order_cost(4) would store. Give thinking time and collect reasons, without recording scores. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Exit explanation
body: Explain how zero travels through your modules.
Name one failed test and its correction.
slides.notes: Look for successful conversion, accepted range, returned zero cost and actual retest evidence. Keep storage integration for the next workshop. Use the response to select the next explanation or practice activity. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

lessons.title: Storage and recovery workshop
lessons.prepare: Open the design chapter and its learning resources. Use paper or a local editor as appropriate, with fictional data and disposable practice copies. The suggested 55-minute lesson is flexible.

slides.title: Storage and recovery workshop
body: Unit 1 · Week 9 · Lesson 4
Save accepted orders and preserve earlier records.
slides.notes: Explain the goal and the expected independent outcome. Save accepted orders and preserve earlier records. This is ungraded textbook learning. Suggested times can be adjusted to the class. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Retrieval and explanation
body: What does append mode retain?
When should an order enter the session list?
slides.notes: Append retains earlier file text. Follow the project contract: successful saving precedes adding the accepted order to the session list. Allow silent thinking before discussion. Ask a learner to justify an answer before revealing the explanation. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Storage checks
table: Clear failure and no false success
slides.notes: Use only disposable synthetic files. Check the agreed CSV fields and record separator in the starter. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Two runs, two records
body: Predict the file after saving quantities 2 and 5.
Compare append with write mode.
slides.notes: With the agreed newline format, append gives two records. Opening in w truncates existing contents. Demonstrate only in a disposable folder. Pause for predictions before discussing the expected result. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: A failed save
body: A save function reports failure.
Trace whether the session list should change.
slides.notes: It should remain unchanged under this project contract. Do not claim success or create a summary entry for an unsaved order. Swap explaining and checking roles so both learners articulate the reasoning. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Independent practice
body: Connect storage to your accepted-order workflow.
Test two runs and a simulated save failure.
Keep a safe copy before changing files.
slides.notes: Use a stub returning False or the supplied controlled failure fixture. Do not change OS permissions on important files. Check before/after session state and file contents. Offer the relevant worked example if needed, then use a changed case to check independent understanding. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: A choice to explain
body: Only the newest order survives the second run.
A: Inspect the file mode and record-writing path.
B: Add more input prompts.
slides.notes: A addresses the reported storage failure. Verify a correction with two runs rather than changing unrelated interface behaviour. Give thinking time and collect reasons, without recording scores. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.

slides.title: Exit explanation
body: Show the retained records from two runs.
Explain the outcome when saving fails.
slides.notes: Expected: both valid records remain and a failed save does not falsely enter session data. Unfinished work becomes a specific next action. Use the response to select the next explanation or practice activity. Teaching reference: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/#design. Use the current chapter and its linked resources.
